\chapter{Day}
\label{ch:te-day}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} in Telugu and choose between the everyday Persian loan and its formal Sanskrit alternate.}

Say \te{రోజు}, a genuine Persian loan from rōz, and set it against the formal \te{దినము} — the mirror image of Kannada's plain dina.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rōju]{\te{రోజు} (rōju) — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} a genuine Persian surprise}

\label{lesson:TE-C23-roju}



\begin{quote}
You might expect Telugu's word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} to be Sanskrit, like Kannada's \emph{dina}, or native Dravidian. It's neither — it's Persian.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{రోజు}} (\textbf{rōju}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is Telugu's everyday, ordinary word for \textquotedblleft{}a day.\textquotedblright{} Here's the real surprise: it's \textbf{borrowed from Classical Persian} \textbf{\ar{روز}} (\emph{rōz}) — the same root, ultimately, as the Persian day names hiding in words like \textquotedblleft{}Nowruz\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}new day\textquotedblright{}). Persian \emph{rōz} itself traces to a Proto-Indo-European root, \emph{\textbf{*lewk-}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bright}\textquotedblright{}) — a \textbf{completely different} PIE root from the \emph{\textbf{*dyew-}} family behind Latin's \emph{diēs}, Hindi's \emph{din}, and Kannada's \emph{dina}. Both roots independently mean something like \textquotedblleft{}shining, bright\textquotedblright{} — but they are \textbf{not} cousins; this is convergent meaning, not shared ancestry.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Telugu also has \textbf{\te{దినము}} (\textbf{dinamu}) — the same Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama} word as Kannada's \emph{dina}. But here's the honest twist: unlike Kannada, where \emph{dina} is the plain, everyday word, Telugu's \textbf{\te{దినము}} is the more \textbf{formal, literary} alternate — \emph{rōju} does the everyday work instead. Telugu's formal/everyday split runs the \textbf{opposite direction} from Kannada's.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rōju\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} a genuine Persian loanword
  \item the honest surprise — from Persian rōz, PIE \emph{lewk-, NOT the same root as diēs/din/dina}
  \item the reversed pattern — dinamu is Telugu's FORMAL word, unlike Kannada's plain dina
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What language does Telugu's everyday \textbf{\te{రోజు}} (\emph{rōju}) come from? (\textbf{Persian} — \emph{rōz}.) Is Persian \emph{rōz}'s PIE root the same as Latin \emph{diēs}/Hindi \emph{din}/Kannada \emph{dina}'s root? (\textbf{No} — a completely different PIE root, \emph{*lewk-}, \textquotedblleft{}bright,\textquotedblright{} vs. \emph{*dyew-} — related in meaning, not in ancestry.) Is Telugu's Sanskrit word, \emph{\te{దినము}} (\emph{dinamu}), the everyday word or the formal one? (\textbf{The formal one} — the opposite of Kannada, where \emph{dina} is plain and everyday.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṇa]{\te{ణ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S126-letter-nna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ఎ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{ఘ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ణ}}
\textbf{\te{ణ}} — \emph{ṇa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṇ}, it is \textbf{ṇa}.

There is a second \emph{n} in this alphabet, and you met it long ago: \textbf{\te{న}}, the \emph{na} of \emph{nēnu} and \emph{namaskāram}. For \te{న} the tongue touches the back of the teeth. For \textbf{\te{ణ}} it curls back and touches the roof of the mouth. Telugu hears the two as different letters and writes them as different letters — the same split you have already seen between \textbf{\te{ల}} and \textbf{\te{ళ}}, and between \textbf{\te{ద}} and \textbf{\te{డ}}. The dot under the romanized \emph{ṇ} is how this book marks the curled-back one.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ణ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వాతావరణం}} \emph{vātāvaraṇam} — weather
  \item \textbf{\te{శ్రావణం}} \emph{Śrāvaṇaṁ} — the fifth of the twelve months
  \item \textbf{\te{ఫాల్గుణం}} \emph{Phālguṇaṁ} — the twelfth
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ణ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ణ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two, and say which one has \te{ణ} and which has \te{న}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{వాతావరణం}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ణ} three times, saying \emph{ṇa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{ణ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ణ}? What sound does it carry, and where is the tongue for it? (\emph{\textbf{ṇa}}, with the tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth — not \te{న}, which touches the teeth.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

One more, from much earlier: \te{ల} — what does it do?
\end{tcolorbox}
